verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Jalandhar footwear component and sports-leather makers with tight monthly stock and receivable controls; avoid small tanneries and export-only units with weak effluent compliance.
title: Jalandhar Leather & Footwear: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Jalandhar's leather and footwear cluster runs on small units converting hides and synthetic uppers into shoes, sports goods and components, and cash turns on the working-capital cycle, not on fixed assets.** Value sits in the cutting, stitching and finishing stages; the tanner upstream carries the effluent and chemical cost, the assembler downstream carries the brand and retail margin. **So when a proposal lands, check where the borrower sits in that chain before you look at turnover.**

## What has changed now
**The local support system is weak: Punjab's only government leather and footwear institute in the city has two regular teachers against 19 sanctioned posts and 25 students against 120 seats [1].** That is a skills pipeline problem, not a demand problem, and it is a September 2026 report. Against it, the state signed an MoU to boost the Jalandhar sports and leather industry [2] and a Rs 10 crore R&D centre was announced in January 2026 [3] — both are announcements, not yet cash flows. **Punjab GST collections are running +9.7% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D], so local demand is holding; but India-wide exports are -3.0% Apr-to-date in USD [D], so the export leg is the weak one.**

## Where the growth is
**Pursue the domestic-facing component and sports-leather supplier who sells to branded footwear and sports-goods assemblers, and the unit that can show a purchase order from a brand.** Peer data shows sector quarterly sales up 13.68% YoY with net margin 6.65% and D/E 0.16 [5], and Bata's volume-led growth [6] tells you volumes are moving through organised retail. **Avoid the pure export converter with no domestic order book, and avoid any tanning unit whose effluent consent you cannot see — ICRA flags pollution-limit lapses as a direct credit risk [10].**

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the cycle: cash credit sized to stock and receivables, not to turnover, with a stock-and-receivables statement every month.** Take monthly GST returns, monthly stock statement, and quarterly debtor ageing; ask for the effluent consent renewal date at sanction. **If gearing crosses the peer norm of 0.16 [5], ask for the debt schedule and the promoter contribution before enhancing limits.** Rating evidence shows a footwear maker's PBILDT falling from Rs 28.13 crore to Rs 18.69 crore year-on-year with gearing still at 0.09 [9] — margin can compress even when the balance sheet looks clean, so price the limit for that.

## Early warning signs
**Watch for a shift from domestic orders to export-only billing, a fall in monthly GST turnover, and rising receivable days.** If the borrower's export share rises while India-wide exports stay at -3.0% [D], ask for the buyer-wise order book. If monthly stock statements stop matching GST turnover, freeze the drawing power. **Collect from customer: actual effluent consent status, buyer concentration, and receivable days — the sources do not give city-level figures for these.**
